provenance.method: lesson notes written from the NERDC 2025 scheme of work outline; every week keeps its scheme topic and bullets as the teaching spine

topics.title: The Cell and Its Functions
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to state the cell theory, identify organelles in a cell, differentiate between plant and animal cells, and observe cells under a microscope.

Introduction:
We have learned about living things and their characteristics. Today we will explore the smallest unit of life, the cell, which is the building block of all living organisms.

Content:
Cell theory states that all living things are made up of cells, the cell is the basic unit of life, and all cells come from pre-existing cells. In our bodies, cells are like the small rooms in a building - each has a special job. Organelles are tiny structures within a cell that perform specific functions. For example, the nucleus is like the king of the cell, controlling all activities. Mitochondria are like power houses, producing energy for the cell. The cell membrane is like the security guard, controlling what enters and leaves the cell. Plant cells have a cell wall, which is like a strong fence providing extra support, and chloroplasts for making food. Animal cells don't have these structures. In Nigeria, we can compare cells to the small shops in a market - each has a specific function but all work together to make the market successful.

Class activity:
Students will prepare and observe onion skin cells and cheek cells under the microscope. They will draw and label the parts they observe.

Evaluation questions:
1. State the three parts of cell theory.
2. Name two organelles found in plant cells but not in animal cells.
3. Explain the function of the mitochondrion.
4. How is a cell membrane similar to a security guard at a gate?
5. Why do you think plant cells have a cell wall but animal cells do not?

Summary:
The cell is the basic unit of life with specialized structures called organelles that perform specific functions for the cell to survive and work properly.

topics.title: Tissues and Organs
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to define tissues, list different types of tissues, explain the functions of various tissues, and describe how organs work together in systems.

Introduction:
Last week we learned about cells, the smallest units of life. Today we will see how these cells group together to form tissues and how tissues come together to make organs.

Content:
Tissues are groups of similar cells that work together to perform a specific function. In our bodies, tissues are like different sections of a market - all the tomato sellers together form one tissue, all the fish sellers form another. There are four main types of tissues in animals: epithelial tissue covers body surfaces, muscle tissue helps in movement, connective tissue supports and binds other tissues together, and nervous tissue transmits messages. In plants, there are meristematic, protective, parenchyma, collenchyma, and sclerenchyma tissues. Organs are made up of different tissues working together. For example, the stomach is an organ made of muscle tissue for movement, epithelial tissue for lining, and connective tissue for support. Just like the different sections of a market work together to make the market function, organs work together in organ systems to perform complex functions.

Class activity:
Students will create a model of an organ using colored paper to represent different tissues and explain how these tissues work together.

Evaluation questions:
1. Define tissue and give an example.
2. List the four main types of animal tissues.
3. Explain how tissues work together to form an organ.
4. Why is coordination important between different organ systems?
5. Compare plant tissues to animal tissues.

Summary:
Tissues are groups of similar cells that work together, and organs are made up of different tissues that perform specific functions in the body.

topics.title: Heredity and Variation
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain the concept of heredity, differentiate between inherited and acquired traits, state the importance of variation, and demonstrate simple genetic inheritance.

Introduction:
We have learned about cells and how they make up tissues and organs. Today we will explore how characteristics are passed from parents to their children and why children look different from their parents and siblings.

Content:
Heredity is the passing of traits from parents to their offspring through genes. In Nigeria, we can see heredity in families where children resemble their parents in features like skin color, hair texture, and height. Inherited traits are characteristics that are passed down through genes, such as eye color or blood type. Acquired traits are characteristics that develop during a person's life due to environmental factors or personal habits, like a scar from an injury or speaking multiple languages. Variation is important because it allows organisms to adapt to different environments and ensures the survival of species. For example, in a population of beans, some may be resistant to drought while others are not, ensuring that some beans will survive during dry seasons. Simple genetic inheritance can be shown using Punnett squares to predict the probability of offspring inheriting certain traits. For instance, if both parents have brown eyes (dominant trait), their children are more likely to have brown eyes.

Class activity:
Students will create a family tree showing inherited traits for three generations and identify examples of variation within the family.

Evaluation questions:
1. Define heredity and give an example.
2. Differentiate between inherited and acquired traits.
3. Why is variation important for the survival of species?
4. Use a Punnett square to show the possible offspring of two parents with heterozygous traits.
5. Give an example of variation in plants common in Nigeria.

Summary:
Heredity is the passing of traits from parents to offspring, and variation ensures diversity within a species, which is crucial for adaptation and survival.

topics.title: Adaptation of Organisms
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to define adaptation, give examples of adaptations, explain how organisms adapt to their habitats, and differentiate between structural and behavioral adaptations.

Introduction:
We have learned about heredity and variation. Today we will explore how living things adapt to their environments to survive and thrive in different habitats.

Content:
Adaptation is a characteristic that helps an organism survive in its environment. In Nigeria, we see adaptations in many organisms. For example, the camel is adapted to desert environments with its hump for storing fat and ability to go without water for long periods. Organisms adapt to their habitats through structural and behavioral adaptations. Structural adaptations are physical features that help an organism survive, like the long neck of a giraffe to reach high leaves or the thick fur of a polar bear to stay warm in cold climates. Behavioral adaptations are actions that organisms take to survive, like birds migrating to warmer climates during the harmattan season or nocturnal animals being active at night to avoid the heat during the day. Adaptations are important because they increase an organism's chances of survival in its specific environment. For example, the acacia tree has long thorns to protect itself from being eaten by animals in the savanna.

Class activity:
Students will research and present on an organism found in Nigeria and its adaptations to survive in its environment.

Evaluation questions:
1. Define adaptation and give an example.
2. Explain how the camel is adapted to desert environments.
3. Differentiate between structural and behavioral adaptations.
4. Give an example of a structural adaptation in a Nigerian animal.
5. Why are adaptations important for the survival of organisms?

Summary:
Adaptations are characteristics that help organisms survive in their environments, and they can be structural or behavioral in nature.

topics.title: MID-TERM EXAMINATION
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to demonstrate understanding of topics covered in Weeks 1-4 through written examination.

Introduction:
Today we will have our mid-term examination to assess your understanding of the topics we have covered so far this term.

Content:
The examination will cover the following topics: The Cell and Its Functions, Tissues and Organs, Heredity and Variation, and Adaptation of Organisms. Students will be tested on their knowledge of cell theory, organelles, differences between plant and animal cells, tissues and their functions, organs and organ systems, heredity, inherited and acquired traits, variation, and adaptations. The examination will consist of multiple-choice questions, short-answer questions, and diagram labeling. Students should review their notes, textbooks, and any class activities to prepare for the examination.

Class activity:
Students will complete the mid-term examination under supervised conditions.

Evaluation questions:
The mid-term examination will serve as the evaluation for this week.

Summary:
The mid-term examination assesses students' understanding of the topics covered in the first four weeks of the term.

topics.title: MID-TERM BREAK
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to rest and recharge for the second half of the term.

Introduction:
After weeks of hard work, it is time for a break to rest and prepare for the remaining part of the term.

Content:
This is a holiday period for students to rest, relax, and engage in recreational activities. Students are encouraged to use this time to revise what they have learned so far and prepare for the topics to be covered in the remaining weeks of the term. Teachers may assign light reading or research activities to keep students engaged during the break. It is important for students to maintain some level of academic activity during the break to prevent forgetting important concepts learned in class.

Class activity:
Students will enjoy their break and engage in recreational activities that help them relax and recharge.

Evaluation questions:
No formal evaluation during the break period.

Summary:
The mid-term break provides an opportunity for students to rest and prepare for the second half of the term.

topics.title: Atoms and Molecules
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to describe the basic structure of an atom, differentiate between elements, compounds, and mixtures, write symbols and formulae, and balance simple chemical equations.

Introduction:
We have learned about living organisms and their adaptations. Now we will explore the building blocks of all matter, both living and non-living - atoms and molecules.

Content:
An atom is the smallest unit of an element that retains its properties. Atoms are made up of even smaller particles: protons (positive charge), neutrons (no charge), and electrons (negative charge). The protons and neutrons are found in the nucleus at the center of the atom, while electrons orbit around the nucleus. Elements are pure substances made up of only one type of atom. For example, gold is made up of only gold atoms, and oxygen is made up of only oxygen atoms. Compounds are substances made up of two or more different elements chemically combined in fixed ratios. Water is a compound made of hydrogen and oxygen atoms in a 2:1 ratio. Mixtures are combinations of two or more substances that are not chemically combined and can be separated by physical means. In Nigeria, we see mixtures in everyday life, like the combination of garri and water, or the different ingredients in a pot of jollof rice. Chemical symbols are abbreviations used to represent elements, such as H for hydrogen, O for oxygen, and Na for sodium. Chemical formulae represent the composition of compounds, like H₂O for water. Simple chemical equations show how substances change during chemical reactions, like the burning of kerosene in a stove: C₁₀H₂₂ + 31O₂ → 20CO₂ + 22H₂O.

Class activity:
Students will build models of atoms using different colored balls to represent protons, neutrons, and electrons, and create a chart showing the symbols of common elements.

Evaluation questions:
1. Describe the basic structure of an atom.
2. Differentiate between elements, compounds, and mixtures.
3. Write the symbols for the following elements: gold, carbon, nitrogen.
4. What is the chemical formula for water and what does it tell us?
5. Balance the following simple equation: H₂ + O₂ → H₂O.

Summary:
Atoms are the basic building blocks of matter, and they combine to form elements, compounds, and mixtures that make up all substances around us.

topics.title: Changes in Matter
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to differentiate between physical and chemical changes.
The students should be able to identify reversible and irreversible processes in everyday life.
The students should be able to explain simple experiments demonstrating changes in matter.

Introduction:
We have learned about different types of matter in our previous lessons. Today we will explore how matter can change in different ways.

Content:
Physical changes are changes that affect the form of a substance, but not its chemical composition. For example, when water freezes into ice, it is still water, just in a solid form. In Nigeria, during the harmattan season, you might see water in a bucket turning into ice if the temperature drops low enough. Another example is when you bend a metal spoon, it changes shape but is still the same metal.

Chemical changes are changes that produce new chemical substances. For example, when wood burns, it turns into ash and smoke, which are new substances. In our local markets, when fish is smoked for preservation, it undergoes a chemical change that gives it a different taste and helps it last longer.

Reversible processes are changes that can be undone. For example, when you melt ice to water, you can freeze the water back into ice. In our homes, when we boil water in a kettle to make tea, the steam can be condensed back into water if cooled properly.

Irreversible processes are changes that cannot be undone. For example, when an egg is cooked, it cannot be turned back into a raw egg. When we burn kerosene in our stove for cooking, it cannot be turned back into kerosene once it has been burned.

Simple experiments to demonstrate changes in matter include:
1. Melting ice: Place ice in a beaker and heat it gently. The ice melts into water, showing a physical change.
2. Burning paper: Burn a small piece of paper. It turns into ash and smoke, showing a chemical change.
3. Dissolving salt in water: Mix salt in water and then let the water evaporate. The salt remains, showing a reversible physical change.

Class activity:
Divide students into small groups. Give each group a piece of chalk and a piece of paper. Ask them to crush the chalk and tear the paper. Then have them write observations about whether these changes are reversible or irreversible and whether they are physical or chemical changes.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is the difference between a physical change and a chemical change?
2. Give one example of a reversible change and one example of an irreversible change.
3. When you cook beans, is this a physical or chemical change? Explain your answer.
4. Why is it important to understand changes in matter in our daily lives?

Summary:
Today we learned about physical and chemical changes, reversible and irreversible processes, and how to identify them in our everyday lives.

topics.title: Water and Air
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to state the composition and importance of water and air.
The students should be able to explain methods of water purification and conservation.
The students should be able to demonstrate understanding of air pressure through simple experiments.

Introduction:
We use water and air every day for various purposes. Today we will learn more about what they are made of and why they are important to us.

Content:
Water is made up of hydrogen and oxygen atoms combined in a ratio of 2:1. It is essential for all living things. In Nigeria, water is used for drinking, cooking, farming, and many other purposes. Without water, plants cannot grow, and animals cannot survive. Our bodies are made up of about 60% water, which helps regulate our body temperature and transport nutrients.

Air is a mixture of gases, mainly nitrogen (about 78%), oxygen (about 21%), and small amounts of other gases like carbon dioxide and argon. We need oxygen from the air to breathe and stay alive. In our crowded danfo buses in Lagos, the air can become stuffy because there is not enough fresh air circulating.

Water purification is the process of removing harmful substances from water to make it safe for drinking. In Nigeria, some common methods include boiling, filtering, and using water treatment chemicals. Many families in rural areas use sand filters to purify their drinking water. Boiling water for at least 10 minutes is one of the most effective ways to kill harmful microorganisms.

Water conservation means using water wisely to avoid waste. In Nigeria, during the dry season, water can be scarce, so it's important to conserve it. Simple ways to conserve water include turning off the tap while brushing teeth, fixing leaky taps, and using water from washing vegetables to water plants.

Air pressure is the force exerted by air on objects. It's what makes a balloon inflate when you blow air into it. In Nigeria, during the harmattan season, the air pressure can be higher, making the air feel dry and cool. Simple experiments to demonstrate air pressure include:
1. Balloon experiment: Blow up a balloon and observe how it expands due to air pressure.
2. Glass and card experiment: Fill a glass with water, place a card on top, and turn it upside down. The card stays in place due to air pressure.

Class activity:
Students will work in groups to design a simple water filter using materials like plastic bottles, sand, gravel, and charcoal. They will test their filters by pouring dirty water through them and observing the results.

Evaluation questions:
1. What are the main components of water and air?
2. Describe two methods of water purification used in Nigeria.
3. Why is water conservation important in Nigeria?
4. How does air pressure affect the weather during harmattan season?

Summary:
Today we learned about the composition and importance of water and air, methods of water purification and conservation, and how air pressure works through simple experiments.

topics.title: Microorganisms and Diseases Vaccination and hygiene practices
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify different types of pathogens and how they cause diseases.
The students should be able to explain methods of disease transmission.
The students should be able to describe prevention and control measures for common diseases.

Introduction:
We have learned about different types of living things. Today we will focus on tiny living things called microorganisms that can cause diseases.

Content:
Microorganisms are tiny living organisms that cannot be seen with the naked eye. They include bacteria, viruses, fungi, and protozoa. Some microorganisms are helpful, like those that help us digest food, but others can cause diseases. In Nigeria, many common diseases like malaria, typhoid fever, and cholera are caused by microorganisms.

Pathogens are microorganisms that cause diseases. Bacteria are single-celled organisms that can reproduce quickly in the body. Viruses are even smaller than bacteria and need a living host to reproduce. Fungi can cause skin infections like ringworm. Protozoa are single-celled organisms that can cause diseases like malaria, which is a big problem in many parts of Nigeria.

Disease transmission is how microorganisms spread from one person to another. Common ways include:
1. Direct contact: Touching an infected person, like when someone with a cold sneezes on you.
2. Indirect contact: Touching surfaces contaminated with microorganisms, like doorknobs in public places.
3. Through the air: Breathing in droplets from coughs and sneezes.
4. Through water and food: Drinking contaminated water or eating food prepared in unhygienic conditions.

Prevention and control of diseases involve good hygiene practices. In Nigeria, some important practices include:
1. Handwashing: Washing hands with soap and clean water, especially before eating and after using the toilet.
2. Proper sanitation: Using clean toilets and disposing of waste properly to prevent contamination of water sources.
3. Vaccination: Getting vaccinated against diseases like measles, polio, and COVID-19.
4. Using treated bed nets: Sleeping under insecticide-treated bed nets to prevent mosquito bites that cause malaria.
5. Keeping food covered: Storing food properly to prevent contamination by flies and other insects.

Vaccination is a method that helps our bodies build immunity against specific diseases. When you get vaccinated, your body learns to fight the disease without getting sick. In Nigeria, the government provides free vaccines for children against many dangerous diseases through the Expanded Programme on Immunization.

Class activity:
Students will create posters showing different disease prevention methods. They will include illustrations and brief explanations of why each method is important.

Evaluation questions:
1. Name four types of microorganisms that can cause diseases.
2. Describe three ways diseases can be transmitted.
3. Why is vaccination important in preventing diseases?
4. What are some good hygiene practices that can help prevent the spread of diseases in Nigeria?

Summary:
Today we learned about microorganisms and diseases, how they are transmitted, and the importance of prevention and control measures like vaccination and good hygiene.

topics.title: REVISION
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to recall key concepts from all topics covered in Term 2.
The students should be able to apply their knowledge to solve related problems.

Introduction:
We have covered many important topics this term. Today we will revise what we have learned to prepare for our examination.

Content:
Let's review the main topics we studied this term:

1. Changes in Matter: We learned about physical and chemical changes, reversible and irreversible processes. Remember that physical changes affect form but not composition, while chemical changes create new substances. For example, when you cook jollof rice, it's a chemical change because the ingredients combine to create something new with different properties.

2. Water and Air: We studied their composition and importance, water purification methods, and air pressure. Water is essential for life and must be purified to remove harmful substances. Air pressure affects weather patterns and can be demonstrated through simple experiments like the balloon and glass experiments.

3. Microorganisms and Diseases: We identified different pathogens, how they transmit diseases, and prevention methods. Good hygiene practices like handwashing and vaccination are crucial for preventing the spread of diseases in our communities.

To help you remember these concepts, let's think about everyday examples:
- When rain falls on dry ground during harmattan season and then evaporates, it's a reversible physical change.
- The water we get from the borehole in our village needs to be purified through boiling or filtering before drinking.
- Mosquitoes transmit malaria, which is why we use treated nets and clean our surroundings to prevent breeding sites.

Class activity:
Students will work in teams to create mind maps of the three main topics covered this term. Each team will present their mind maps to the class, explaining the key points and connections between concepts.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is the difference between a physical change and a chemical change? Give an example of each.
2. Why is water purification important in Nigeria?
3. Name three ways diseases can be transmitted and how to prevent each.
4. How does air pressure affect our daily lives?

Summary:
Today we revised the main topics covered in Term 2, including changes in matter, water and air, and microorganisms and diseases. Understanding these concepts will help you perform well in your examination.

topics.title: EXAMINATION
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to demonstrate their understanding of all topics covered in Term 2.
The students should be able to apply scientific knowledge to solve problems in the examination.

Introduction:
Today is your end of Term 2 examination. This assessment will test your understanding of all the topics we have covered this term.

Content:
The examination will cover all topics taught in Term 2, including:

1. Changes in Matter: Questions will test your understanding of physical and chemical changes, reversible and irreversible processes. You may be asked to identify examples of each type of change and explain why they belong to that category.

2. Water and Air: Questions will focus on the composition and importance of water and air, water purification methods, and air pressure. You may need to explain why water purification is important in Nigeria and describe methods used locally.

3. Microorganisms and Diseases: Questions will assess your knowledge of pathogens, disease transmission, and prevention methods. You may be asked to identify different types of microorganisms and describe how they cause diseases.

The examination will consist of multiple-choice questions, short answer questions, and one or two extended response questions. Read each question carefully before answering. Manage your time wisely, spending more time on questions that carry more marks.

Remember to:
- Read all instructions carefully before starting.
- Write your name and class clearly on your answer sheet.
- Answer all questions to the best of your ability.
- Show your working for calculation questions.
- Check your answers before submitting your paper.

Class activity:
The examination itself is the main activity for this week. Students will work individually to complete the examination paper within the allocated time.

Evaluation questions:
The evaluation questions are the examination questions themselves, which will cover all topics taught in Term 2.

Summary:
Today you are taking your end of Term 2 examination. This assessment will help demonstrate your understanding of the scientific concepts we have studied this term. Do your best and remember to manage your time wisely.

topics.title: CLOSING/VACATION
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to reflect on their learning experiences during Term 2.
The students should be able to set goals for personal improvement in the next term.

Introduction:
Today marks the end of Term 2. We have learned many interesting scientific concepts together.

Content:
As we close this term, let's reflect on what we have learned:

1. We explored changes in matter, understanding how physical and chemical changes affect our daily lives. We conducted experiments to see how matter can change form or create new substances.

2. We studied water and air, learning about their composition, importance, and how to keep them clean. We designed water filters and discussed the importance of water conservation in Nigeria.

3. We learned about microorganisms and diseases, discovering how tiny organisms can cause illnesses and how we can protect ourselves through good hygiene and vaccination.

During the vacation, I encourage you to:
- Review your notes and textbooks to reinforce what you have learned.
- Observe the world around you and try to identify examples of the scientific concepts we studied.
- Read science-related books or watch educational programs to expand your knowledge.
- Prepare for Term 3 by looking at the topics you will be studying.

Remember that science is all around us. Whether you're cooking in the kitchen, playing outside, or traveling in a danfo bus, you can observe scientific principles at work. Stay curious and keep asking questions about how the world works.

Class activity:
Students will write a short paragraph about their favorite topic from Term 2 and why they found it interesting. They will also share one thing they would like to learn more about in science.

Evaluation questions:
1. What was your favorite topic in Term 2 and why?
2. How will you use what you learned in science this term in your daily life?
3. What scientific topic would you like to explore more during the vacation?

Summary:
Today we concluded Term 2 and reflected on our learning experiences. Have a wonderful vacation and come back ready for new scientific discoveries in Term 3.
